text.p: The European Commission on Tuesday counter-attacked against allegations that it had mishandled the mad cow crisis.

Lars Hoelgaard, a senior veterinary official, rejected a charge by German veterinary expert Oscar Riedinger that it failed to deal adequately with meat and bone meal, which is held responsible for spreading mad cow disease.

Last week Riedinger told the European Parliament's committee of inquiry into the disease, known as bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), that the Commission failed to insist on higher standards in fighting the disease.
"The accusation is untrue, is false and the whole attack is somewhat misguided," Hoelgaard told a news conference.
Hoelgaard, the Commission's link with the parliament committee, said only high risk cattle parts, such as brain and spinal cord, were given high pressure heat and chemical processing.
Low risk cattle or sheep tissue, whether in Britain or in other EU member states, including Germany, was not subject to such stringent processing standards, he added.
"Therefore the accusation that we have been undermining this so-called German standard is inconsistent and doesn't stand up," he said.
He urged the parliamentary committee to organise a direct confrontation between Riedinger and all the EU scientists involved in dealing with cattle rendering.
Hoelgaard also strongly attacked European gelatine manufacturers for withholding important information on the public health risk of gelatine manufacturing methods.

"It's a disgrace...undermining their own credibility, withholding information relevant for the scientists and therefore also reflecting negatively and totally unjustifiably on what the Commission had done," Hoelgaard said.
